items.stem: A student's laptop is on wifi and showing a web page from another website. No course software is running on it. Is the laptop acting as a server at this moment?

options.text: No. It is acting as a client, because no program on it is waiting for requests.
options.feedback: A computer is a server only while a program on it is waiting for connections. Here the laptop is sending requests and receiving pages, which makes it a client.

options.text: Yes. Any computer connected to a network is a server.
options.feedback: Being on a network is not enough. A server is a program that waits for requests, and nothing is waiting on this laptop.

options.text: Yes. It has a processor and memory, which is all a server needs.
options.feedback: Every computer has a processor and memory. What makes a computer a server is the program running on it.

options.text: No. Only machines in a data center can be servers.
options.feedback: Any computer can be a server, including a laptop or a Raspberry Pi, as long as a program is waiting for connections.

items.stem: In the address `https://enlist.edu:443/api/courses`, which part tells the client which program on the machine to talk to?

options.text: `:443`, the port
options.feedback: A port number identifies one program among the many that may be listening on the same machine.

options.text: `enlist.edu`, the host
options.feedback: The host says which machine to contact. It does not say which program on that machine.

options.text: `/api/courses`, the path
options.feedback: The path names a resource inside the program that is already chosen.

options.text: `https`, the scheme
options.feedback: The scheme says which rules to use for the conversation, such as encrypted HTTP. It does not pick the program.

items.stem: Before you try it: your laptop runs the course tool on port 8080. A classmate on the same wifi types `localhost:8080` in their browser. What do they see?

options.text: Nothing from your laptop. Localhost points to their own computer.
options.feedback: Localhost always means the computer you type it on. They need your local network address, such as `192.168.1.7:8080`.

options.text: Your course tool, because you are on the same wifi.
options.feedback: Sharing wifi helps only if they use your network address. Localhost never leaves their own machine.

options.text: Your course tool, but only if you turn off your router.
options.feedback: Switching off the router does not change what localhost means.

options.text: An error from the university's public server.
options.feedback: Localhost does not point to any public server. It points to the computer that is typing it.

items.try: Choose "A classmate on the same wifi" in the "Who can reach what" widget above and compare.

items.stem: Your laptop's wifi address is `192.168.1.7`. A friend in another city types that number to reach your laptop. Why does it fail?

options.text: It is a private address used in millions of homes, so it is meaningless online.
options.feedback: Private ranges such as `192.168.x.x` are reused inside many networks. No router on the internet can tell which one you mean.

options.text: The address has not been registered with DNS for outside visitors.
options.feedback: DNS turns names into numbers. A number you type directly does not need DNS, and a private number would still be unreachable.

options.text: Your laptop only has a public address, and your friend typed the wrong one.
options.feedback: Your laptop has no public address of its own. The public address belongs to your router and is shared by everyone in the building.

options.text: The friend must first enter your wifi password on their device.
options.feedback: A password controls who joins your wifi. It does not make a private address reachable from outside.

items.stem: Select all that apply. Which of these stop a home laptop from serving a public website reliably?

options.text: Its address is private and sits behind a router shared with the building.
options.feedback: The internet cannot route to a private address, so outside visitors cannot reach the laptop.

options.text: Its address can change at any time.
options.feedback: Home connections are often given a new address, so a site that depends on one fixed address stops working.

options.text: Home plans are slow to upload, and serving a site is all upload.
options.feedback: Every page sent to a visitor is upload traffic, and home plans give much less upload speed than download speed.

options.text: A laptop cannot run a program that listens for connections.
options.feedback: A laptop can run such a program, so it meets the definition of a server.
